entities.summary:
The Battle of Plataea was a pivotal land battle fought on August 479 BCE in Plataea, Greece, between the Persian Empire and a coalition of Greek city-states. The battle marked a decisive victory for the Greeks, led by the Spartans, who had been resisting the second Persian invasion of Greece. This victory allowed the Greeks to gain control of their city-states and paved the way for the development of the Golden Age of Athens, which saw significant cultural, philosophical, and artistic achievements. The battle also had a profound impact on the course of Western civilization, shaping the trajectory of European history and influencing the rise of the Roman Empire.

The battle itself was a brutal and bloody conflict, with the Greeks employing a clever tactic to defeat the numerically superior Persian forces. The Greek army, led by the Spartan general Pausanias, used a clever defensive strategy to protect their flanks and then launched a surprise counterattack, catching the Persians off guard and leading to a decisive victory. The battle resulted in heavy casualties for the Persians, with estimates suggesting that up to 40,000 Persian soldiers were killed or wounded.

The legacy of the Battle of Plataea can be seen in the development of the Greek city-states, which went on to become major players in the ancient world. The battle also had a lasting impact on the course of Western civilization, shaping the trajectory of European history and influencing the rise of the Roman Empire. The battle is still remembered today as a pivotal moment in the struggle for Greek independence and a testament to the bravery and cunning of the Spartan warriors.

The Battle of Plataea serves as a reminder of the enduring power of human ingenuity and determination in the face of overwhelming odds. As the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote, 'The victory of the Greeks was due to the bravery and cunning of their leaders, who were able to outwit the Persians and secure a decisive victory.'
